title: The Reach Is Part of the Workout
subtitle: For people with COPD, arm-related breathlessness can shape everyday life. Pulmonary rehabilitation can address upper-body function, but the best approach is the one a person and their care team can make workable.
imageAlt: Two friends sit at a kitchen table, helping a woman with COPD make a list of everyday tasks she wants to discuss with her pulmonary-rehabilitation team.

body: The work hidden in an ordinary reach

A cupboard door, a freshly washed shirt, a pan lifted from the stove: daily life asks the arms to reach, carry, push and hold. For a person with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), some of those moments may also bring breathlessness. That can make upper-body tasks feel demanding in a way that is easy for other people to miss. It is not a character flaw or evidence that someone simply needs to try harder. It is useful information about how the person is managing the activities that matter to them.

Strength training is often discussed through numbers—weight lifted, repetitions completed, or progress measured over time. In COPD rehabilitation, upper-limb work has another important frame: what happens when someone reaches for a shelf, washes their hair or puts groceries away? Starting with a person’s own daily activities can give a rehabilitation conversation a clear purpose without turning a diagnosis into a generic workout plan.
Why arm function belongs in rehabilitation

Pulmonary rehabilitation is a clinician-guided program of care, not just a set of exercises to copy at home. The American Thoracic Society recommends it for adults with stable COPD and for adults with COPD after hospitalization for an exacerbation. Its guideline describes rehabilitation as an important part of care, while leaving room for a program to reflect the needs and circumstances of the individual [1].

For some people, a meaningful goal may involve walking farther or recovering more comfortably after exertion. For others, it may be making a particular upper-body task less disruptive. Both belong in a discussion about function. The point is not that arm training replaces other parts of rehabilitation, or that every person with COPD needs the same emphasis. It is that upper-body demands can be named and considered alongside the rest of a person’s goals.

A 2025 randomized trial compared two forms of upper-limb muscle training within a four-week pulmonary-rehabilitation program. The single-center study included 280 people with COPD. Breathlessness improved in both the force-training and endurance-training groups, and the researchers found no significant difference between the groups in improvement in dyspnea. Biceps strength increased more in the force-training group. At the same time, a higher proportion of people in that group could not reach the required intensity because they found the program too difficult [2].

Those results do not identify a universal winner. They show that different outcomes can point in different directions: one approach produced a greater increase in a specific strength measure, while breathlessness improvement did not differ significantly between approaches, and tolerability mattered. A program that someone cannot manage at the intended intensity may not be a good fit simply because one measure improved more. The study is one piece of evidence, not a promise about what any individual will experience.
A useful distinction: strength, endurance and the task

Strength and endurance are related but not interchangeable. A person may want to build the ability to produce force, sustain arm activity, or manage a particular movement with less interruption. The task itself can help clarify what is relevant: Is it the reach to a high shelf? Holding the arms up while grooming? Carrying a light object across a room? Naming the activity does not diagnose the reason it feels difficult; it gives the rehabilitation team a concrete starting point.

A 2023 systematic review examined 24 studies involving 882 people with COPD. It found very-low- to low-certainty evidence that resistance-based upper-limb training may improve upper-limb strength compared with lower-limb exercise alone or no exercise. It did not find significant differences among the upper-limb training types it compared. The review also noted limitations in study quality and risk of bias [3]. In plain terms, upper-limb work may have a role, but the evidence does not settle which format is best for everyone.

Before a rehabilitation visit, a person who wants to can jot down two or three arm-related activities that feel important. Keep the description ordinary and precise: “I get short of breath while putting away dishes,” or “I avoid reaching into the closet because it takes a lot out of me.” Note when the difficulty occurs and what would make the activity more manageable from the person’s point of view. There is no need to assign a score or arrive with a training solution.

Then ask the rehabilitation clinician how the program could address those activities, what kind of upper-limb work is being considered, and how the team will judge whether it is a good fit. It is reasonable to ask how the plan can be adjusted if the work feels too difficult, what signs should prompt a pause or check-in, and how progress will be discussed. Those are questions for the care team, which can account for a person’s health and program—not instructions to improvise an exercise routine.

A friend or relative can make the conversation easier if the person with COPD wants that support. They might help write down the activities the person names, accompany them to an appointment, or help remember the clinician’s explanation. The person living with COPD sets the agenda and decides what role, if any, a companion should have. A supportive partner does not need to coach movements, set training intensity or turn ordinary household tasks into tests.

That distinction matters. An activity list is not a demand to perform every task more often, and a loved one’s observations should not displace the person’s account of their own experience. A companion can ask, “Would it help if I wrote that down?” or “Do you want me to come with you?” If the answer is no, respecting it is part of useful support.
A plan built around real life

Upper-body rehabilitation is most useful as a conversation about fit: what a person wants to do, what the team recommends, and what can be sustained within an individualized program. Research offers reasons to consider arm function, but it also shows why sweeping claims about one best method are premature. The 2025 trial found improvements in breathlessness in both groups without a significant difference between them, while strength and difficulty reaching the prescribed intensity distinguished the groups in other ways [2]. The systematic review likewise found limited certainty and no clear advantage among the upper-limb training types it examined [3].

The practical next step is modest: name one task that matters, bring it to the pulmonary-rehabilitation team, and ask how the program can address it safely and realistically. The goal is not to make a person’s daily life prove their fitness. It is to let the life they want to lead help guide the rehabilitation conversation.
